paras: The Stanaford City killings took place at daybreak on February 25, 1903, when joint posses under Deputy U.S. Marshal D. W. Cunningham and Sheriff Harvey Cook shot and killed three Black men in the house of Stonewall Jackson at Stanaford City, Raleigh County, West Virginia, during a battle with striking coal miners. A coroner's jury found that one of the dead, William Clark, had been feloniously shot by men under Cunningham's direction. A union investigator said the men were shot in their beds without warning, but a federal grand jury exonerated the officers and indicted miners, Jackson among them.

The posses were sent to arrest miners charged with violating Federal Judge B. F. Keller's blanket injunction against New River coal strikers. On February 21 armed miners ordered Cunningham out of Atkinsville when he came to serve writs, and Sheriff Cook was turned away the same way. Told to serve the process 'at all hazards', Cunningham returned with Cook and about a hundred armed men.

The posses surrounded the village at daylight and sent squads to the houses where they believed the wanted men were staying. In the grand jury's account, Jackson slammed his door on the first demand and fired a shotgun at posse member Edward D. Summers, the posse returned fire, and 'two or three' of the eleven men inside were killed. Union investigator Chris Evans said instead that Jackson's wife, four children and eight men were asleep when shots were fired in from outside without a word, leaving William Dodson, William Clark and Richard Clayton dead on the floor. Ada Jackson told the coroner's inquest that there was 'no call to surrender' and that she heard someone outside say 'Kill the last one.'

Elsewhere Joseph Hizer was shot through a window while dressing, and his sister testified that Cunningham told her 'Women and children must take care of themselves.' About 1,500 to 2,000 shots were fired across the town, no officers were hurt, and 73 men were arrested.

The coroner's jury found Clark 'feloniously shot' by men under Cunningham's direction but could not say whether Clayton and Dodson were killed lawfully. Federal court officers then ordered the surviving victims not to talk to newspapermen. A federal grand jury indicted 'Stonewall Jackson (colored)' and others for resisting officers at Atkinsville and returned over 250 indictments against miners, but none against the deputy marshal or his guards. Its report, laid before President Roosevelt, found that Cunningham had acted 'in a prudent and conservative manner'.

When the strike ended in July, the Huntington Advertiser noted that the union's protest to Roosevelt and Attorney General Knox had produced nothing definite. No report of a trial of any posse member appears in the coverage.

The first Charleston dispatch, printed on February 26 from Birmingham and New York to Louisville and St. Louis, gave the officers' story of 'rioting miners' and did not mention race. Headlines read 'Strikers Fire on Deputies' in the New-York Tribune and 'Miners Opened Fire 300 Strong' in the Wheeling Register. West Virginia papers split, the Pocahontas Times calling the strikers 'a menace to society' while Morgantown's Daily New Dominion called it a 'massacre' and wrote that 'Somebody ought to be hanged for this affair.'

Evans's report brought the race of the dead into headlines such as 'Investigation of the Killing of Negro Miners' and 'MINERS SHOT IN BED. NO MERCY FOR WOMEN.' The grand jury's findings then ran as 'EXONERATES MARSHAL' and 'COMPLETE VINDICATION', and the report itself complained of 'gross misrepresentations' in the newspapers.

In the Black press the Richmond Planet put the story on its front page on March 14 as 'KILLED IN THEIR BEDS', using the same syndicated text a Delaware weekly had printed the day before. The Savannah Tribune gave it one line in a news digest, and no Black-press editorial on the killings was found.

The officers said the posse fired only after Jackson shot at Summers, while Evans and Ada Jackson said the shooting began without warning. Death counts range from three killed in the first wire, which named different dead, to eight in the Pocahontas Times. Evans placed the felonious-killing verdict on Dodson's death, but the printed verdict names Clark.

reader.title: Stanaford City killings
bases: Joint posses of a deputy U.S. marshal and the Raleigh County sheriff, serving federal writs during a coal strike, shot and killed three Black men in Stonewall Jackson's house (A11, A22, A7).

The officers' grand jury report, the UMW investigator, Ada Jackson's inquest testimony and the coroner's verdict all agree that posse gunfire killed men in Jackson's house at daybreak, though they disagree on who fired first (A22, A11, A16, A7).

accounts.label: First Charleston wire (officers' version)
accounts.gist: The posses surprised rioting miners in camp at daybreak and called on them to surrender; the reply was a shot, and in the battle three miners were killed and two mortally wounded.

accounts.label: Federal grand jury
accounts.gist: At the first house, Jackson slammed the door and fired a shotgun at Summers; the posse returned fire and two or three inmates were killed; the posse fired only after being fired on.

accounts.label: UMW investigator Chris Evans
accounts.gist: Shots were fired into Jackson's house at daybreak without warning, killing three men in bed or dressing; no one was asked to surrender until after the shooting began, and only one house returned fire.

accounts.label: Ada Jackson at the coroner's inquest
accounts.gist: There was no call to surrender, only shooting; a bullet passed her face, she heard 'Kill the last one', and later found three men dead on the floor.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: William Clark was feloniously shot by armed men under Cunningham's direction; it could not say whether Clayton and Dodson were killed lawfully.

accounts.label: Pocahontas Times (posse-side local account)
accounts.gist: Yeager's squad came on a camp of negro strikers and several were killed before they surrendered; eight dead and nine wounded in all.

framing.detail: First-day wires spoke of 'rioting miners' and headlines such as 'Strikers Fire on Deputies' and 'Miners Opened Fire 300 Strong', with no mention of race.
The Pocahontas Times called the strikers 'a menace to society' and praised posse leaders' 'conspicuous bravery'.
Morgantown's Daily New Dominion called it 'the massacre in Stannaford city' and wrote 'Somebody ought to be hanged for this affair.'
After the Evans report and Ada Jackson's testimony, headlines read 'Miners Shot in Bed' and 'Investigation of the Killing of Negro Miners'.
Coverage of the grand jury ran under 'EXONERATES MARSHAL' and 'COMPLETE VINDICATION'.
The Richmond Planet ran the syndicated Evans story on its front page as 'KILLED IN THEIR BEDS'; the Savannah Tribune gave it one line in a digest; no Black editorial comment was found.

conflicts.note: Same-day wires datelined Feb. 25 and the grand jury report both give Feb. 25; the Evening World's Feb. 26 stands alone.
